claim: Animal sociality emerges from individual decisions on how to balance the costs and benefits of being sociable.
source: Animal sociality emerges from individual decisions on how to balance the costs and benefits of being sociable.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on animal sociality and decision-making.

claim: Novel pathogens introduced into wildlife populations should increase the costs of sociality, selecting against gregariousness.
source: Novel pathogens introduced into wildlife populations should increase the costs of sociality, selecting against gregariousness.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on established understanding of disease transmission and social behavior.

claim: Novel pathogen introduction provokes the rapid evolutionary emergence and coexistence of distinct social movement strategies.
source: Using an individual-based model that captures essential features of pathogen transmission among social hosts, we show how novel pathogen introduction provokes the rapid evolutionary emergence and coexistence of distinct social movement strategies.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Distinct social movement strategies differ in how they trade the benefits of social information against the risk of infection.
source: These strategies differ in how they trade the benefits of social information against the risk of infection.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the model results showing different strategies with different preferences for handlers and non-handlers.

claim: Pathogen-risk-adapted populations move more than their pathogen-risk-naive ancestors.
source: Overall, pathogen-risk-adapted populations move more and have fewer associations with other individuals than their pathogen-risk-naive ancestors, reducing disease spread.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and described in the results.

claim: Pathogen-risk-adapted populations have fewer associations with other individuals than their pathogen-risk-naive ancestors.
source: Overall, pathogen-risk-adapted populations move more and have fewer associations with other individuals than their pathogen-risk-naive ancestors, reducing disease spread.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E and described in the results.

claim: Reduced associations in pathogen-risk-adapted populations reduce disease spread.
source: Overall, pathogen-risk-adapted populations move more and have fewer associations with other individuals than their pathogen-risk-naive ancestors, reducing disease spread.
evidence: This is demonstrated through network epidemiological models run on emergent social networks (Figure 5B).

claim: Host evolution to be less social can be sufficient to cause a pathogen to be eliminated from a population.
source: Host evolution to be less social can be sufficient to cause a pathogen to be eliminated from a population, which is followed by a rapid recovery in social tendency.
evidence: This is shown in scenario 2 results (Figure 7A).

claim: Pathogen elimination is followed by a rapid recovery in social tendency.
source: Host evolution to be less social can be sufficient to cause a pathogen to be eliminated from a population, which is followed by a rapid recovery in social tendency.
evidence: This is shown in scenario 2 results where handler-tracking strategy recovers after pathogen extinction (Figure 7A).

claim: Animal associations can yield useful social information about resource availability.
source: Such associations can yield useful social information whether inadvertently or deliberately transmitted about resource availability (Danchin et al., 2004; Dall et al., 2005; Gil et al., 2018), but they also provide opportunities for the transmission of parasites and infectious pathogens among associating individuals (Weinstein et al., 2018; Romano et al., 2020; Albery et al., 2021a; Cantor et al., 2021; Romano et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on social information.

claim: Animal associations provide opportunities for the transmission of parasites and infectious pathogens among associating individuals.
source: Such associations can yield useful social information whether inadvertently or deliberately transmitted about resource availability (Danchin et al., 2004; Dall et al., 2005; Gil et al., 2018), but they also provide opportunities for the transmission of parasites and infectious pathogens among associating individuals (Weinstein et al., 2018; Romano et al., 2020; Albery et al., 2021a; Cantor et al., 2021; Romano et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on disease transmission in social animals.

claim: Wildlife pathogen outbreaks affect most animal taxa, including mammals.
source: Wildlife pathogen outbreaks affect most animal taxa, including mammals (Blehert et al., 2009; Fereidouni et al., 2019; Chandler et al., 2021; Kuchipudi et al., 2022), birds (Wille and Barr, 2022), amphibians (Scheele et al., 2020), and social insects (Goulson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies of wildlife disease outbreaks.

claim: Wildlife pathogen outbreaks affect birds.
source: Wildlife pathogen outbreaks affect most animal taxa, including mammals (Blehert et al., 2009; Fereidouni et al., 2019; Chandler et al., 2021; Kuchipudi et al., 2022), birds (Wille and Barr, 2022), amphibians (Scheele et al., 2020), and social insects (Goulson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to work on avian disease.

claim: Wildlife pathogen outbreaks affect amphibians.
source: Wildlife pathogen outbreaks affect most animal taxa, including mammals (Blehert et al., 2009; Fereidouni et al., 2019; Chandler et al., 2021; Kuchipudi et al., 2022), birds (Wille and Barr, 2022), amphibians (Scheele et al., 2020), and social insects (Goulson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to work on amphibian disease.

claim: Wildlife pathogen outbreaks affect social insects.
source: Wildlife pathogen outbreaks affect most animal taxa, including mammals (Blehert et al., 2009; Fereidouni et al., 2019; Chandler et al., 2021; Kuchipudi et al., 2022), birds (Wille and Barr, 2022), amphibians (Scheele et al., 2020), and social insects (Goulson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to work on insect disease.

claim: Movement decisions incorporating social information can facilitate or reduce spatial associations.
source: Movement decisions incorporating social information the presence and status of neighbours can facilitate or reduce spatial associations and help animals balance the costs and benefits of sociality (Albery et al., 2021a; Gil et al., 2018; Webber and Vander Wal, 2018; Webber et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on movement and social information.

claim: Animals' social movements link landscape spatial structure, individual distributions, and the emergent structure of animal societies.
source: Animals' social movements link landscape spatial structure, individual distributions, and the emergent structure of animal societies (Gil et al., 2018; Webber et al., 2023; Kurvers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on movement ecology and social structure.

claim: Social movements influence the dynamics of disease outbreaks in animal populations.
source: Together, they influence the dynamics of disease outbreaks in animal populations (White et al., 2018b; Romano et al., 2020; Romano et al., 2022; Keeling et al., 2001), and such outbreaks may in turn have cascading effects on landscape structure and community ecology (Monk et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on disease dynamics.

claim: Disease outbreaks may have cascading effects on landscape structure and community ecology.
source: Together, they influence the dynamics of disease outbreaks in animal populations (White et al., 2018b; Romano et al., 2020; Romano et al., 2022; Keeling et al., 2001), and such outbreaks may in turn have cascading effects on landscape structure and community ecology (Monk et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to work on ecological consequences of disease.

claim: Animal pathogen outbreaks can reduce social interactions among individuals over ecological timescales of a few months or years.
source: Over relatively brief ecological timescales of a few months or years, animal pathogen outbreaks can reduce social interactions among individuals due to a combination of factors.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent explanation and citations in the paragraph.

claim: Mortality from disease may induce decreases in population density, leading to fewer associations.
source: For instance, mortality from the disease may induce decreases in population density (e.g. Fereidouni et al., 2019; Monk et al., 2022), leading to fewer associations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Adaptive behavioural responses by which animals identify infected individuals can trigger quarantining or self-isolation behaviours that reduce encounters between infected and healthy individuals.
source: Furthermore, adaptive behavioural responses by which animals identify infected individuals (and indeed, whether they are themselves infected) can trigger quarantining or self-isolation behaviours that reduce encounters between infected and healthy individuals overall (Stroeymeyt et al., 2018; Pusceddu et al., 2021; Stockmaier et al., 2021; Weinstein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies of behavioral responses to infection.

claim: When pathogens are first introduced into a population, fine-tuned avoidance responses are less likely, as individuals may have no prior experience of cues that indicate infection.
source: When pathogens are first introduced into a population, such as during novel cross-species spillover (Kuchipudi et al., 2022; Chandler et al., 2021), fine-tuned avoidance responses are less likely, as individuals may have no prior experience of cues that indicate infection (Weinstein et al., 2018; Stockmaier et al., 2021; although general cues of infection may still play a role; see Townsend et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations and logical inference about novel pathogen encounters.

claim: A novel pathogen spreading through host–host contacts and imposing costs upon infected individuals could confer an evolutionary advantage upon less social individuals if these are also less frequently infected.
source: A novel pathogen spreading through host–host contacts and imposing costs upon infected individuals could thus confer an evolutionary advantage upon less social individuals if these are also less frequently infected.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on evolutionary principles.

claim: It is a common expectation that pathogen introduction broadly selects against host social behaviour, and hence against social connectivity itself.
source: Therefore, it is a common expectation that pathogen introduction broadly selects against host social behaviour, and hence against social connectivity itself (Altizer et al., 2003; Cantor et al., 2021; Romano et al., 2022; Poulin and Filion, 2021; Ashby and Farine, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical and empirical work.

claim: The transmission of foraging tactics depends on social interactions.
source: Important aspects of animal ecology, including the transmission of foraging tactics (Klump et al., 2021) and migration routes (Jesmer et al., 2018; Guttal and Couzin, 2010), depend on social interactions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The transmission of migration routes depends on social interactions.
source: Important aspects of animal ecology, including the transmission of foraging tactics (Klump et al., 2021) and migration routes (Jesmer et al., 2018; Guttal and Couzin, 2010), depend on social interactions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Climate change is expected to make novel pathogen introductions more common.
source: Climate change is only expected to make novel pathogen introductions more common (Sanderson and Alexander, 2020; Carlson et al., 2022a), making such studies more urgent.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on climate change and disease.

claim: Novel pathogen introductions are primarily studied for their immediate demographic implications.
source: Despite this salience, novel pathogen introductions are primarily studied for their immediate demographic (Fey et al., 2015), and potential medical (Wille and Barr, 2022; Chandler et al., 2021; Kuchipudi et al., 2022; Levi et al., 2012) and economic implications (Keeling et al., 2001; Goulson et al., 2015; Jolles et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Most introductions of novel pathogens into wildlife only come to light when they result in mass mortality events.
source: Indeed, most introductions of novel pathogens into wildlife only come to light when they result in mass mortality events (Fey et al., 2015; Wille and Barr, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical observations.

claim: Host evolutionary dynamics are mostly ignored in studies of novel pathogen introductions.
source: Host evolutionary dynamics (and especially changes in sociality) are mostly ignored, and this is presumably because the evolution of pathogen host traits, and moreover complex behavioural traits such as sociality, is expected to be slow and not immediately relevant for management.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the field with an inference about the reason.

claim: Theory suggests that animal sociality evolves to balance the value of social associations against the risk of pathogen transmission.
source: Theory suggests that animal sociality evolves to balance the value of social associations against the risk of pathogen transmission (Bonds et al., 2005; Prado et al., 2009; Ashby and Farine, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Analytical models often reduce animal sociality to single parameters.
source: However, analytical models often reduce animal sociality to single parameters, while it actually emerges from individual decisions conditioned on multiple internal and external cues.
evidence: This is a critique of existing analytical models based on knowledge of the field.

claim: Social decision-making and movement often vary among individuals.
source: Social decision-making and movement often also vary among individuals (Tanner and Jackson, 2012; Wolf and Weissing, 2012; Spiegel et al., 2017; Gartland et al., 2022), but analytical models are unable to include individual differences in sociability.
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical and theoretical work.

claim: Analytical models are unable to include individual differences in sociability.
source: Social decision-making and movement often also vary among individuals (Tanner and Jackson, 2012; Wolf and Weissing, 2012; Spiegel et al., 2017; Gartland et al., 2022), but analytical models are unable to include individual differences in sociability.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of analytical models.

claim: Network models often cannot capture fine-scale feedbacks between individuals' social and spatial positions.
source: Yet network models often cannot capture fine-scale feedbacks between individuals' social and spatial positions (Albery et al., 2021a; Albery et al., 2021b), nor spatial variation in infection risk (Albery et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work discussing limitations of network models.

claim: Networks constructed from relatively low-resolution spatial relocation data may be sensitive to the network formation process when seeking to understand the rapid spread of diseases.
source: Networks constructed from relatively low-resolution spatial relocation data (such as infrequent direct observations; see e.g. Albery et al., 2021b), may be sensitive to the network formation process when seeking to understand the rapid spread of diseases, especially if transmission has a non-linear relationship with association strength (Farine, 2017; White et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological work on network construction.

claim: Adding an explicit spatial setting to movement-disease models can be valuable in gaining a more general understanding of the interplay between social decisions, movement, and pathogen transmission.
source: Consequently, adding an explicit spatial setting to movement-disease models can be valuable in gaining a more general understanding of the interplay between social decisions, movement, and pathogen transmission (He et al., 2021; Scherer et al., 2020; White et al., 2018c; White et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Individual-based simulation models can incorporate substantial ecological detail, including explicit spatial settings.
source: IBMs can incorporate substantial ecological detail, including explicit spatial settings (DeAngelis and Diaz, 2019), and detailed disease transmission dynamics (White et al., 2018a; Scherer et al., 2020; Lunn et al., 2021; White et al., 2018c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior IBM work.

claim: Individual-based models can include individual decision-making, allowing ecological and epidemiological outcomes to emerge from individuals' movement choices.
source: Most importantly, IBMs can include individual decision-making, allowing ecological and epidemiological outcomes to emerge from individuals' movement choices.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of IBMs based on knowledge of the modeling approach.

claim: Individual-based models hitherto have focused on immediate epidemiological outcomes and do not have an evolutionary component examining long-term consequences.
source: Individual-based models hitherto have focused on immediate epidemiological outcomes, such as infection persistence, and do not have an evolutionary component examining long-term consequences for either pathogens or their hosts (White et al., 2018a; Scherer et al., 2020; Lunn et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior IBM work and identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: Introducing an infectious pathogen to 4% of individuals in each generation leads to a rapid evolutionary shift that is complete within only 100 generations of pathogen introduction.
source: Introducing an infectious pathogen to 4% (n = 20) of individuals in each generation (after G = 3000) leads to a rapid evolutionary shift that is complete within only 100 generations of pathogen introduction in how social information is incorporated into individual movement strategies.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and described in the results section.

claim: The frequency of agent-avoiding and handler-tracking strategies is comparable within 500 generations, and fluctuates thereafter.
source: The frequency of agent-avoiding and handler-tracking strategies is comparable within 500 generations, and fluctuates thereafter, with increases in one strategy corresponding to decreases in the other.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and described in the results section.

claim: After pathogen introduction, there is an increase in the average importance of individuals' preferences for the presence of other foragers.
source: After pathogen introduction, there is an increase in the average importance of individuals' preferences (or aversions) for the presence of other foragers, that is, the importance of social cues (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and described in the results section.

claim: There is significant variation among individuals in the importance of social cues to their movement strategies after pathogen introduction.
source: Additionally, there is significant variation among individuals in the importance of social cues to their movement strategies, with distinct evolved polymorphisms that vary substantially between simulation replicates (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and described in the results section.

claim: There is a sharp increase in the mean distance moved by individuals after pathogen introduction.
source: There is a sharp increase in the mean distance moved by individuals; while pre-introduction individuals moved 52% of their lifetimes on average, post-introduction, individuals move for about 62% of their lifetimes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and described in the results section.

claim: The evolutionary shift in social movement strategies does not lead to a reduction in mean per-capita intake.
source: Surprisingly, this does not lead to a reduction in mean per-capita intake (Figure 2D, green), but there is a sharp drop in mean per-capita energy (intake – total infection cost) due to the cost of infection (Figure 2D, purple).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and described in the results section.

claim: There is a sharp drop in mean per-capita energy due to the cost of infection after pathogen introduction.
source: Surprisingly, this does not lead to a reduction in mean per-capita intake (Figure 2D, green), but there is a sharp drop in mean per-capita energy (intake – total infection cost) due to the cost of infection (Figure 2D, purple).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and described in the results section.

claim: The emergence of avoidant strategies leads to a fivefold drop in encounters between individuals after pathogen introduction.
source: The emergence of avoidant strategies leads to a fivefold drop in encounters between individuals after pathogen introduction (Figure 2E), which suggests that most encounters were indeed likely taking place on or near resource clusters.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E and described in the results section.

claim: Agent-avoiding individuals move more than handler-tracking or agent-tracking foragers.
source: For example, the population-level increase in movement after pathogen introduction is shown to be due to the increase in frequency of the agent-avoiding strategy as these individuals move more than handler-tracking or agent-tracking foragers (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and described in the results section.

claim: Agent-avoiding individuals have a lower intake than either handler-tracking or agent-tracking individuals.
source: Simultaneously, agent-avoiding individuals have a lower intake than either handler-tracking or agent-tracking individuals which have similar intakes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and described in the results section.

claim: All three strategies have comparable net energy and hence equivalent fitness.
source: Despite this, all three strategies have comparable if not identical net energy and hence equivalent fitness this is to be expected given their coexistence (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and described in the results section.

claim: The relationship between movement and the mean number of per-capita associations of each strategy is broadly a quadratic one.
source: The shape of the movement–association curve is broadly a quadratic one (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and described in the results section.

claim: Agent-avoiding and handler-tracking individuals have differing mean infection rates.
source: These differences likely explain why agent-avoiding and handler-tracking individuals have differing mean infection rates, at ∼25 and ∼33%, respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E and described in the results section.

claim: Pre-introduction populations are spatially clustered near food item patches.
source: Pre-introduction populations are spatially clustered near food item patches (Figure 4A) due to movement strategies that favour grouping with successful foragers.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and described in the results section.

claim: Pathogen-risk-adapted populations are more dispersed over the landscape.
source: Pathogen-risk-adapted populations are more dispersed over the landscape, with many individuals found far from food item clusters (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and described in the results section.

claim: Pre-introduction individuals encounter somewhat more unique neighbours than pathogen-risk-adapted individuals.
source: Pre-introduction individuals encounter somewhat more unique neighbours (C, blue) than pathogen-risk-adapted individuals (C; red).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and described in the results section.

claim: The distribution of the individual reproductive number is left-skewed, with most infections not resulting in any secondary cases, but has a long right-hand tail.
source: Individual reproductive number distributions from both intervals are strongly left-skewed but have long right-hand tails (up to 12 just after introductions begin; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and described in the results section.

claim: A small number of infected individuals are responsible for a large number of infections, suggesting that superspreading emerges from the spatial-social dynamics encoded in the model.
source: While most infected individuals do not infect any of their neighbours, a small number of these are responsible for a disproportionately large number of further infections, even after the population has adapted to moving under the risk of transmission (Figure 4D); this is consistent with the phenomenological definition of superspreading (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and described in the results section, with reference to the definition of superspreading.

claim: A large majority of individuals in the generations just after pathogen introduction are infected (≈75%).
source: A large majority of individuals in the generations just after pathogen introduction are infected (≈75%; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and described in the results section.

claim: The number of infected individuals falls to below 50% within 100 generations after pathogen introduction.
source: However, tracking the evolutionary change in movement strategies, the number of infected individuals falls to below 50% within 100 generations (Figure 5A), remaining low for the rest of the simulation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and described in the results section.

claim: Both the single-encounter and multiple-encounter diseases would infect >75% of individuals overall when spreading through the networks of pre-introduction populations.
source: Both the single-encounter and multiple-encounter diseases would infect >75% of individuals overall when spreading through the networks of pre-introduction populations (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and described in the results section.

claim: Pathogen-risk-adapted populations' social networks are more resilient to the multiple-encounter infection compared to their pre-introduction, pathogen-risk-naive ancestors.
source: Pathogen-risk-adapted populations' social networks are however more resilient to the multiple-encounter infection compared to their pre-introduction, pathogen-risk-naive ancestors as these social networks are sparser and individuals are more weakly connected (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and described in the results section.

claim: Landscape productivity does not appear to have an effect on the evolution of social movement strategies.
source: We expected that this would lead to greater handler-tracking persisting on lower productivity landscapes, but did not find this to be case; indeed, there did not appear to be an effect of productivity on the evolution of social movement strategies (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and described in the results section.

claim: The pathogen is successfully transmitted from parents to offspring in the initial generations following the introduction event in scenario 2.
source: The pathogen is successfully transmitted from parents to offspring in the initial generations following the introduction event and among individuals of the same generational cohort.
evidence: This is described in the results section for scenario 2.

claim: In some replicates of scenario 2, the population is slow to transition away from sociality, and the agent-avoiding strategy becomes common only after 200 generations.
source: In some replicates, the population is slow to transition away from sociality, and the agent-avoiding strategy becomes common only after 200 generations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and described in the results section.

claim: In some replicates of scenario 2, the pathogen persists among social individuals for over 500 generations.
source: In such cases, the pathogen persists among social individuals for over 500 generations (panel Pathogen persistence).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and described in the results section.

claim: In some replicates of scenario 2, when the population undergoes a rapid evolutionary shift and agent avoidance becomes common within 100 generations, the number of infections falls rapidly.
source: In contrast, when the population undergoes a rapid evolutionary shift and agent avoidance becomes common within 100 generations, the number of infections falls rapidly.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and described in the results section.

claim: In some replicates of scenario 2, infections drop to zero, which drives the pathogen extinct, following which there is an extremely rapid recovery in the frequency of the more social handler-tracking strategy.
source: In some cases, infections drop to zero, which drives the pathogen extinct following which there is an extremely rapid recovery in the frequency of the more social handler-tracking strategy, and the near-complete extinction of agent-avoiding foragers.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and described in the results section.

claim: Infection cost and the probability of vertical transmission together influence whether populations undergo evolutionary transitions that lead to pathogen elimination.
source: Infection cost and the probability of vertical transmission together influence whether populations undergo evolutionary transitions that lead to pathogen elimination.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B and described in the results section.

claim: Pathogen elimination is more common when pathogen costs are higher.
source: In general, pathogen elimination is more common when pathogen costs are higher (as infected individuals have fewer offspring), and when the probability of vertical transmission is low.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B and described in the results section.

claim: The model is broadly robust to implementing large-scale natal dispersal, with the evolutionary outcomes very similar to those seen in the default implementation with small-scale natal dispersal.
source: We found that our model is broadly robust to implementing large-scale natal dispersal, with the evolutionary outcomes very similar to those seen in our default implementation with small-scale natal dispersal (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9A and described in the results section.

claim: Landscape spatial structure influences the mixture of social movement strategies evolved before pathogen introductions.
source: Landscape spatial structure influences the mixture of social movement strategies evolved before pathogen introductions (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10A and described in the results section.

claim: On the uniform landscape, handler-tracking was the most common strategy before pathogen introduction.
source: On the uniform landscape, handler-tracking was the most common strategy before pathogen introduction, with nearly all individuals of this strategy.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10A and described in the results section.

claim: On the more patchy landscape, the indiscriminately social agent-tracking strategy was the most common before pathogen introductions.
source: In contrast, on the more patchy landscape, the indiscriminately social agent-tracking strategy was the most common before pathogen introductions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10A and described in the results section.

claim: Following pathogen introduction, populations on both uniform and patchy landscapes undergo a rapid evolutionary transition to a mixture of handler-tracking and agent-avoiding strategies.
source: Following pathogen introduction, populations on both landscapes undergo a rapid evolutionary transition to a mixture of handler-tracking and agent-avoiding strategies, which is similar to the change observed in our default scenario (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10A and described in the results section.

claim: When introductions are relatively rare and sporadic, there is no shift in the mixture of movement strategies after pathogen introduction.
source: When introductions are relatively rare and sporadic, there is no shift in the mixture of movement strategies after pathogen introduction. The handler-tracking strategy remains common across parameter combinations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11 and described in the results section.

claim: The mechanistic combination of ecological, evolutionary, and epidemiological dynamics in a spatial setting is unprecedented for host movement-disease models.
source: The mechanistic combination of ecological, evolutionary, and epidemiological dynamics in a spatial setting is unprecedented for host movement-disease models (White et al., 2018b; Manlove et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the approach, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Evolutionary transitions in sociality occur within only a few generations, comparable to the time required for the development of key social aspects of animal ecology, such as migration routes.
source: We demonstrate the pitfalls of this assumption: evolutionary transitions in sociality occur within only a few generations, comparable to the time required for the development of key social aspects of animal ecology, such as migration routes (Jesmer et al., 2018; Cantor et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, supported by comparison to empirical timescales from cited work.

claim: Populations, initially evolved to find patchily distributed food using social information, rapidly evolve to become more sensitive to potential infection risk and eschew social encounters when an infectious pathogen is introduced.
source: We also demonstrate the tension inherent to sociality under the risk of an infectious pathogen in an explicitly spatial context. We show how populations, initially evolved to find patchily distributed food using social information, rapidly evolve to become more sensitive to potential infection risk and eschew social encounters when an infectious pathogen is introduced.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Qualitatively and quantitatively different social movement strategies making different trade-offs between social information and infection risk can coexist in a single population.
source: Our results suggest how qualitatively and quantitatively different social movement strategies making different trade-offs between social information and infection risk can coexist in a single population (Wolf and Weissing, 2012; Webber and Vander Wal, 2018; Gartland et al., 2022; Webber et al., 2023; Wolf et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, supported by citations to prior work on behavioral variation.

claim: Sensitivity to cues of high pathogen transmission risk can rapidly evolve following the introduction of a novel pathogen.
source: Our results show that sensitivity to cues of high pathogen transmission risk can rapidly evolve following the introduction of a novel pathogen.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: The rapid decreases in social interactions should primarily prompt concern that the evolutionary consequences of pathogen introduction could slow the transmission of, and erode, animal culture.
source: Nonetheless, the rapid decreases in social interactions should primarily prompt concern that the evolutionary consequences of pathogen introduction could slow the transmission of, and erode, animal culture (Cantor et al., 2021) including foraging (Klump et al., 2021) and migration behaviours (Jesmer et al., 2018; Guttal and Couzin, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference from the model results, supported by citations to work on animal culture.

claim: Holding the pathogen traits steady and unable to evolve in the course of a simulation is a necessary choice in order to gain first tangible insights from the model.
source: Holding the pathogen traits steady and unable to evolve in the course of a simulation is thus a necessary choice in order to gain these first tangible insights from our model.
evidence: This is a justification for a modeling choice.

claim: Landscape productivity does not strongly influence the evolution of social movement strategies.
source: It is surprising then that landscape productivity does not strongly influence the evolution of social movement strategies, but this may yet be an important factor in enabling high-movement, low-infection strategies when movement is inherently costly.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Across a spectrum of spatial structures, pathogen introduction resulted in a convergence in social movement strategies.
source: However, we found that across a spectrum of spatial structures, pathogen introduction resulted in a convergence in social movement strategies; this evolutionary component may be an important consideration in studies of how spatial structure can influence the spread of infection (He et al., 2021; Scherer et al., 2020; White et al., 2018c; White et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 10, with implications for prior work.

claim: Infection costs affect which social movement strategies evolve in the model.
source: Infection costs do affect which social movement strategies evolve in our model and may help explain intra- and inter-specific diversity in social systems across gradients of infection costs (Altizer et al., 2003; Sah et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 6, with implications for empirical patterns.

claim: Animal populations may be able to adapt relatively quickly to the spillover and eventual persistence of infectious pathogens, even when they cannot specifically detect and avoid infected individuals.
source: Our model suggests that animal populations may be able to adapt relatively quickly to the spillover and eventual persistence of infectious pathogens, even when they cannot specifically detect and avoid infected individuals (Altizer et al., 2003; Stroeymeyt et al., 2018; Stockmaier et al., 2021; Pusceddu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference from the model results, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Population-level behavioural changes could occur even without mortality effects due to evolutionary shifts in sociality alone.
source: Our model shows how population-level behavioural changes could occur even without mortality effects due to evolutionary shifts in sociality alone.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Decreased sociality resulting from adaptation to a novel pathogen could slow the transmission of future novel pathogens.
